description: We’re a team of enthusiastic learners who share a passion for technology, science, and space exploration. Our skills span programming, AI, data analysis, design, and communication. We welcome anyone willing to share knowledge and learn alongside others, whether you’re an expert or just starting out. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to turn ideas into a meaningful, real-world solution through creativity and teamwork.
summary: Evexia is an astronaut health-monitoring web app for long-duration missions. Crew log daily check-ins and wearable readings, and the system flags early signs of cardiovascular, bone and muscle, immune and mood changes against a personal baseline, with clear next steps. Live NASA radiation and solar-event data add mission context. Flight surgeons get a crew dashboard, escalation tracking and role-based access, and an AI assistant explains readings in plain language, and every threshold is labelled as a demonstration value pending clinical validation.
details:
Evexia is a web-based health monitoring system built for astronauts on long-duration missions, where crew must spot changes in their own health without immediate help from Earth.

Crew members record a daily check-in and, where available, readings from a wearable. The app compares each reading with two things: thresholds adjusted for spaceflight, and the person’s own baseline from earlier check-ins. It then gives each indicator a green, amber or red status, explains why it was flagged, and suggests a next step. Patterns across several check-ins, such as repeated fever-range temperatures or sustained short sleep, are also checked, so the app can catch problems a single reading would miss.

Red results are logged as escalations for the flight surgeon. The surgeon’s view shows the whole crew, with a 3D body display for quick status checks, and access depends on role. An AI assistant explains readings in plain language, and a rule-based fallback works without an API key.

Technically, the app uses React and Vite for the interface, Node.js with Express for the server, and SQLite for storage. It draws on NASA radiation (RadLab) and space-weather (DONKI) data, with a script to refresh it, and it includes unit, API, end-to-end and accessibility tests.

The aim is to help crews notice health problems earlier and act sooner, and to show how such a tool could support future missions to the Moon and Mars. Every threshold is labelled honestly as a demonstration value pending clinical validation, and the app is clear that it supports decisions rather than replacing a medical device.
projectRefs: Why Do We Conduct Science Experiments in Space
